findings: Current full-time Dutch BA, RIO 56813, retains a coherent Russian main-language major without stacking branches. The adopted 2026–2027 Appendix 1 and dated list agree on 60+60+60 EC: common 36 plus language 24 in year one, language 12 plus philosophy/Classics/contact 18 plus exchange 30 in year two, and aspect/literature/lab 18 plus free 30 plus thesis 12 in year three. Diagnostic and tutoring zero credits remain separate.

Read actual language and disciplinary prerequisites: Russian 1/2 before 3, 3 before 4, 4 before 5, 5 before 6; Area Studies and Russian 3 before History of Slavic; completed first year before Language Contact; positive BSA before postpropaedeutic study. All are met in the ordinary block order. Full first-year completion meets ordinary 48-EC BSA. Riga specifically requires at least 54 first-year plus 18 year-two semester-one credits including Russian 5/6, met by the full earlier 60+30.

The University of Latvia in Riga is the prescribed Russian host. Exchange follows programme learning lines and nonduplication, with host language courses beyond B1 productive/B2 reading. OER Appendix 1 allows a Board-approved thirty-credit home alternative only for valid inability to travel. This is now stated explicitly without stacking it with exchange. The separate thirty-credit free group retains introductory-level, outside-approval, nonoverlap and at-most-twelve placement-credit rules.

Aspect and post-1950 literature precede Spring Slavic Lab; Russian 6 plus those two are explicit lab requirements. The lab teaches qualitative and quantitative literary/language methods and prepares the thesis proposal. The individual twelve-credit thesis follows the lab and is source-based independent supervised research. Faculty rules normally require programme-language writing with approved exceptions. No invented word count, numeric thesis gate or Scandinavian language clause is imported.

The defining subject is sustained Slavic language, regional literature, cultural history and social inquiry. Classics reads Pushkin, Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, Kundera and Andric in context; modernism and post-1950 literature investigate regional politics, censorship, historical change and distinctive cultures; historical Slavic, contact and aspect connect linguistic inquiry to the selected languages. General humanities methods are genuine parts of the target, not substitutes for its regional object.

All 64 interests were read: sixteen direct/stable generators assigned to three tested directions, thirty-one support topics, six examples and eleven conditional outcomes. No careers generate a curriculum. Three complete feasible trials test language/cultural, literary/historical and political/social priorities. All forty-eight unique UCR course contributions receive substantive weight, including description-only psycholinguistics, literary meaning, policy, social movements, historiography and current American Century research. The excluded Walcheren outline is not used.

Psycholinguistics, stylistics, literary interpretation, historical sources, Soviet documentary, empire, institutions, conflict, social theory and empirical/qualitative methods supply concrete related study. Their combined teaching becomes general humanities or European/global social science rather than sustained Slavic regional inquiry. This no-match is not based on missing language alone, a degree title, professional licence, planning coverage, exact equivalence or a quota of regional courses. All three trial schedules pass actual offerings, prerequisites, four per term, 24 unique, PPD in year one and advanced-course rules.

Read English record/index title, two audience explanations, Russian/Riga label, twenty component names/credits, ten selected notes and all source links through the established exception renderer mapping. The external-only record has no selected UCR programme, concept, block, alignment, optional research or course-description modal. Shared descriptions/app/workbook remain unchanged.
